solution: A rotation of p_1..p_K is the near-identity permutation rho with rho(p_i) = p_{i+1} and rho(p_K) = p_1, because the new teacher-to-class map satisfies new_pos(t) = old_pos(rho(t)). Hence after weeks w1 < w2 < ... the map is rho_{w1} o rho_{w2} o ..., and answering 'teacher d in week x' means starting from d and applying the rotations from the LATEST week at most x downwards. Sqrt-decompose the week axis into blocks of B weeks; each block stores the composition of its plans as a sparse map keyed only on the at most B*K moved teachers. A query applies its own block's plans one by one and then does a single O(1) lookup per earlier block, O(B + M/B); an insertion rebuilds one block in O(B*K). With B about sqrt(M/K) both are O(sqrt(M*K)), so O(Q sqrt(M*K)) time and O(M + Q*K) space. A segment tree fails here: rebuilding the root costs O(Q*K) per insertion.
statement_summary: N teachers start in the classes of the same number and are shuffled by rotations: a plan names up to ten teachers and, from a given week on, moves each into the class the next one occupied. Plans arrive in arbitrary week order interleaved with questions asking which class a teacher holds in a given week, counting only plans issued so far. Up to one hundred thousand operations.
notes: verify_krotating.py reproduces both samples, matches the sqrt structure against a naive replay of all plans on 200 random operation streams, and checks that after every prefix of plans the teacher-to-class map is still a permutation. The composition order is the subtle part: the rotations must be applied newest-first when evaluating at a single teacher. No label for permutation composition exists in the vocabulary.
